subject: Medicine
summary: Chest X‑ray is a bedside tool to identify pneumonia, pleural effusion, cardiac enlargement and other acute thoracic pathology, especially where advanced imaging is unavailable.

sections.p: A chest X‑ray is a two‑dimensional radiographic image of the thorax taken in a postero‑anterior (PA) or anteroposterior (AP) view, used to visualise lung fields, pleura, heart and mediastinum.
b: PA view preferred for accurate heart size
AP view common in bedridden patients

sections.p: Radiographic severity is graded by extent of infiltrates, size of effusion, or cardiothoracic ratio (CTR).
b: CTR ≤ 0.5 = normal; > 0.5 suggests enlargement

sections.p: In low‑resource East African settings the common causes of abnormal CXR are:
b: Pneumonia (bacterial, TB, malaria‑related)
Pleural effusion (TB, heart failure, parapneumonic)
Cardiomegaly (rheumatic heart disease, hypertension, pericardial effusion)
Pulmonary embolism (rarely seen directly, may show Westermark sign)
Aspiration or foreign body (air‑trapping, localized collapse)

sections.p: Clinical clues guide interpretation: fever, cough and focal crackles point to pneumonia; dyspnoea with leg swelling suggests heart failure effusion; sudden unilateral wheeze after choking hints at foreign body.
b: Focal consolidation → air bronchograms
Blunted costophrenic angle → fluid
Mediastinal shift away → large effusion; shift toward → collapse

t.b: Is there a radiographic abnormality explaining the patient’s symptoms? → Detects consolidation, effusion, cardiomegaly, pneumothorax
Is a pleural fluid present and is it simple or complex? → Confirms effusion when X‑ray is equivocal, guides thoracentesis
Is cardiac enlargement due to heart failure or pericardial disease? → Supports cardiac cause when CTR is high
Is the infiltrate infectious (TB, bacterial) ? → Directs antimicrobial therapy

t.a: If X‑ray unavailable: bedside lung ultrasound
t.b: Can it identify B‑lines, pleural effusion or pneumothorax? → Provides rapid alternative in low‑resource settings

sections.p: Unrecognised large effusion or tension pneumothorax can cause rapid respiratory collapse; missed pneumonia may progress to empyema; untreated heart failure leads to pulmonary oedema.
b: Mediastinal shift with respiratory distress → tension physiology
Progressive infiltrates despite antibiotics → empyema
CTR > 0.6 with peripheral oedema → decompensated heart failure

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then address the radiographic abnormality.
b: Pneumonia: empiric antibiotics (e.g., amoxicillin‑clavulanate) after local resistance patterns; avoid macrolides if high QT prolongation risk
Cardiomegaly: optimise heart failure regimen (ACE‑I, diuretics, beta‑blocker) and treat underlying valve disease
Foreign body: urgent bronchoscopy; avoid blind suction

sections.p: Repeat CXR 4‑6 weeks after treatment of pneumonia or effusion to ensure resolution; vaccinate against pneumococcus and influenza; control HIV, TB and malaria to reduce pulmonary complications.
b: Smoking cessation to lower chronic lung disease risk
Regular blood pressure monitoring to prevent cardiac enlargement

sections.p: Radiographic patterns can mimic each other.
b: Pleural effusion vs. lobar collapse (both cause opacity; shift direction differentiates)
Cardiomegaly vs. pericardial effusion (CTR high in both; silhouette sign and echo differentiate)
Pulmonary oedema vs. pneumonia (diffuse interstitial lines vs. focal consolidation)

sections.p: Certain conditions mask typical signs on CXR.
b: Supine film may hide effusion (deep sulcus sign instead of blunting)
Obesity can over‑estimate heart size on AP view
Early TB may show normal CXR despite active disease

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden respiratory distress with mediastinal shift
Severe hypoxia not improving with oxygen
Rapidly enlarging pleural effusion causing hemodynamic compromise

faq.q: Why does a large effusion push the mediastinum away?
faq.a: The fluid occupies space and exerts pressure, displacing mediastinal structures to the opposite side.

faq.q: Can a normal chest X‑ray rule out tuberculosis?
faq.a: No; early pulmonary TB may have a normal CXR, so sputum testing is still required if suspicion is high.

exam: A 65‑year‑old with fever, cough and right‑sided dullness on percussion – what is the next radiographic sign you look for and what does it indicate? — Look for blunting of the right costophrenic angle; it suggests a pleural effusion.

A patient’s CXR shows a unilateral white‑out with mediastinal shift to the opposite side – what is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management? — Large pleural effusion; perform urgent thoracentesis if symptomatic.
You see a meniscus‑shaped opacity with the mediastinum shifted toward the opacity – what alternative diagnosis should you consider? — Lung collapse/atelectasis rather than effusion.

In a bedridden child with suspected pneumonia, only an AP film is available – what limitation does this impose on interpretation? — Heart size appears enlarged; cardiothoracic ratio may be falsely high.

A patient with known rheumatic heart disease has a CTR of 0.58 – what does this tell you and what further test is needed? — Suggests cardiac enlargement; obtain an echocardiogram to assess valve function.
Why might a supine chest X‑ray miss a moderate pleural effusion and what sign can still be seen? — Fluid layers posteriorly, producing a deep sulcus sign (hyperlucent lateral costophrenic area).
A smoker over 50 has a new peripheral opacity on CXR – what follow‑up is recommended? — Repeat CXR in 6 weeks to exclude underlying malignancy.

What radiographic feature distinguishes pulmonary oedema from pneumonia? — Diffuse bilateral interstitial Kerley B lines and perihilar ‘bat‑wing’ pattern versus focal consolidation with air bronchograms.
